Anchor of the Soul
ANG-kur of the SOHL
n. phrase
From the figure of Hebrews 6:19, hope as ankyran tēs psychēs, an anchor of the soul; Greek ankyra (anchor) and psychē (soul), borrowed from the seaman's steadying gear.

See also: Anchor of the Soul

📖 Biblical Definition

The Anchor of the Soul is the scriptural figure for the Christian's hope, set forth in Hebrews 6:19: "Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil." As an anchor steadies a ship against wind and tide, holding her fast amid storm, so the believer's hope steadies the soul against the tempests of affliction, doubt, and temptation, keeping it from being driven and tossed. But the figure is heightened in a wonderful way: this anchor is cast not downward into the shifting seabed below, but upward and inward, "into that within the veil"—into the very holy of holies in heaven, where Jesus the forerunner is for us entered (Heb 6:20). The believer's hope is moored to Christ Himself, seated at the right hand of God within the heavenly sanctuary; the cable runs from the storm-tossed soul on earth to the immovable Savior in glory. The ground of this hope's sureness is twofold: the immutable promise of God and His oath, "two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie" (Heb 6:18), and the entrance of Christ as forerunner, who has gone before to secure the harbor and bring His people safely in. Thus the anchor is "sure and stedfast"—sure in itself, fastened in heaven, and steadfast in its hold, never to drag or slip. This figure undergirds the doctrine of the perseverance of the saints: because the anchor is fixed in Christ within the veil, and not in the believer's own strength, the soul cannot finally be carried away; the same Lord who is the object of the hope is the keeper of the soul that hopes. This dictionary confesses that the believer's hope, grounded in God's oath and moored to the ascended Christ within the veil, is a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, the very ground of his perseverance unto the end.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ANCHOR as an iron instrument for holding a ship at rest in water, and figuratively that which gives stability or security. The Anchor of the Soul is the believer's hope, sure and steadfast, moored to Christ within the veil (Heb 6:19).

expand to see more

ANCHOR, n. — An iron instrument for holding a ship or other vessel at rest in water. Figuratively, that which gives stability or security; that on which we place dependence for safety.

In the spiritual sense, the Anchor of the Soul is the Christian's hope, fastened not in the shifting seabed but in heaven, where Christ the forerunner is entered.

"Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil" (Heb 6:19).

It requires that hope be moored to the ascended Christ and grounded on God's oath; it forbids resting the soul's security on its own strength or feelings.

Being sure and steadfast, the anchor cannot drag or slip—it is the very ground of the believer's perseverance unto the end.

📖 Key Scripture

Hebrews 6:19 — "Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil."

Hebrews 6:18 — "That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us."

Hebrews 6:20 — "Whither the forerunner is for us entered, even Jesus, made an high priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec."

Romans 5:5 — "And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Anchor of the Soul faces no postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is a sure, objective hope moored to the ascended Christ, against the modern reduction of hope to mere optimism or wishful sentiment.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The figure of the anchor stands clear of the culture-war controversies, yet the biblical hope it pictures is widely diluted in modern usage, where "hope" has shrunk to mean a vague optimism, a hopeful feeling, a wish that things may turn out well. So weakened, hope becomes a sentiment as shifting as the sea it is meant to weather, anchored to nothing, holding nothing fast. The positive principle to recover is the objective and sure character of biblical hope: it is not a feeling that the believer generates but a confident expectation grounded on the immutable promise and oath of God, in which it is impossible for Him to lie (Heb 6:18). Hope, biblically, is as certain as the God on whose word it rests.

The greater recovery is the direction and ground of the anchor. The believer's hope is moored not in himself, nor in his circumstances, nor in the visible and shifting things of earth, but "within the veil," in the heavenly sanctuary where Christ the forerunner is entered (Heb 6:19-20). Because the cable runs from the storm-tossed soul to the immovable Savior in glory, the anchor is sure and steadfast and cannot finally slip. This is the ground of the perseverance of the saints: the soul is kept, not by the firmness of its own grip, but by the fixedness of the anchor in Christ. To recover the doctrine is to teach the trembling believer to look away from his own wavering frame to the steadfast object of his hope, and to find his soul held fast by the One who has gone before within the veil.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The figure rests on the ankyra tēs psychēs of Heb 6:19, hope as an anchor sure and steadfast, entering within the veil where Christ the forerunner is gone before.

expand to see more

Greek ankyra (G45) — anchor; the seaman's steadying gear, here the figure of the believer's hope (Heb 6:19).

Greek psychē (G5590) — soul, life; the soul steadied by hope amid the storms of affliction.

Greek elpis (G1680) — hope; the confident expectation grounded on God's oath, not a mere wish.

Greek prodromos (G4274) — forerunner; Christ entered within the veil to secure the harbor for His people (Heb 6:20).

The anchor is moored not below but above, within the veil, fixed in the ascended Christ—the ground of the saints' perseverance.

Usage

"When the storms of affliction beat upon him, his hope held him fast, the Anchor of the Soul, sure and steadfast."

"The Anchor of the Soul is cast not into the shifting seabed but within the veil, moored to the ascended Christ."

"Because the Anchor of the Soul is fixed in Christ and not in the believer's own strength, the saints cannot finally be carried away."
